data.title: Mysterious signs carved into rocks in the Váh region
data.excerpt: At several sites in the north-western Váh region, strange signs carved into the rocks are still waiting for a comprehensive expert study: at Bodiná, at Vlkov in Horná Mariková and on Orgoňova Kýčera. The explanations offered range from the idle work of 17th–18th-century Vlach shepherds through a mysterious Slavic or runic script and a pagan sacrificial site to a schematic map of the surrounding terrain.

children.text: At some sites in the north-western Váh region we find mysterious, artificially made signs carved into the rocks. Experts have so far been unable to prove either their origin or their meaning. Some claim that they are signs carved by Vlach shepherds some time in the 17th–18th centuries, when they were bored while grazing sheep, but there are also those who hold that they are a mysterious Slavic script, or runes.

Thanks to Mr Martin Olšovský and his as yet unpublished book „Znaky a nápisy na skalách v okolí Považskej Bystrice“, we bring you an article in which these mysterious signs, which are still waiting for a comprehensive expert study, are documented in photographs.
BODINÁ (Zálučie, Zadné Hrachoviská) – inscriptions on the rocks

From the lower end of the village, upstream along the brook on the left towards Kostolec and Vrchteplá, 1 km from the village, on the south-western foot of the Mazáková hill /595.4 m a.s.l./, about 15 m above the little brook, there are signs carved into the rocks. The largest, front face of the stone is vertical and about 160 cm high /general view and fig. no. 1/. The other inscribed surfaces are smaller flat stones placed to the left /fig. no. 2/ and to the right /fig. no. 3/, obliquely on the slope. A complete inscription in Cyrillic /no. 4/, REGINA COELI LAETARE, has a longer upper line /32 cm/, the height of the letters being 2.5–3 cm. It is placed on a flat stone about 2 m lower down the slope, below the sign in fig. no. 3. The stones are already considerably weathered and overgrown with moss, the signs indistinct. Without any outside intervention I photographed the site together with the individual inscribed surfaces. With the help of a drawing on paper I reconstructed the signs on the photographs.

blocks.alt: Mysterious signs carved into rocks in the Váh region

children.text: /Martin Olšovský, on Good Friday, 10 April 1998/

„The inscriptions were discovered as early as the last century by Pavol Križko /Sborník Slovenskej muzeálnej spoločnosti, 1896/. He considered them a Slavic script, even though most of them are simple or broken crosses. This problem was also taken up by JUDr. Vojtech Bukovinský, who considered them a runic script and on their basis searched for the so-called milestones of the Amber Road.

More recently the signs from Bodiná have been dealt with by the Czech author Horák in the book „O Slovanech trochu jinak“, who regards them as symbols of human sacrifices that were allegedly carried out here. An explanation of these signs may come in the future, but to judge by one of them on a low stone, which is written in both Cyrillic and Latin letters and reads „Regina coeli laetare“ – We praise the Queen of Heaven, it may be assumed that the signs mentioned above are not so very old either and that they may have been a certain form of expression of religious feeling in the last century, or a place where cult rites as yet unknown to us could have been held.“
/Jozef Moravčík, graduate historian, in a series on the villages of the Považská Bystrica district, the weekly Obzor, 1993-1994./

P.S. The whole inscription REGINA COELI LAETARE is written in Cyrillic; the only Latin letter is the „L“ in the word COELI, if we disregard the letters A, E, O, T, which have the same shapes in both Cyrillic and Latin. The author of the inscription probably did not have a full command of Latin, because in the word „COELI“ he used Č instead of the Russian C.
/note by M. Olšovský/
Horná Mariková – Vlkov – „Skala na kerej smrc spočinula“ (the rock on which death came to rest)

„In Horná Mariková, in the part called Vlkov, there is a rock about which the local people have said from time immemorial that death rested on it. It is evidently meant in the sense that death, on its wanderings about the world, had to rest somewhere too. Originally the rock stood above the road, but when the road was widened it was pushed lower down, so that today it lies above the confluence of the little brook with the main stream from Ráztoka,“ Štefan Meliš, who for many years has been uncovering the secrets of our ancestors, begins his account with a smile.

„Last autumn my acquaintance Gašpar Zemančík heard from a certain man from Vlkov that there were strange signs on a rock in the brook, and he told me this interesting piece of news at once. So we set out for the place together with him to find the signs. When we got there, a rock overgrown with moss was waiting for us. Only when we had removed the moss did we see three signs – a sun, a star and a horseshoe. Several questions occurred to us at once. Was a treasure buried here, or did the rock serve as a landmark, or was it a sacrificial site on which pagans made offerings to the gods? Above the rock, on the left-hand side, at a place called Pekliská, stone was apparently once quarried, so it occurred to us whether the signs might have been cut by the stonemasons, because nearby there are regular rocks of quadrangular shape which they left behind.“
Orgoň’s „runes“ on Kýčera

But this discovery was not the only one. „On Orgoňova Kýčera, on the ridge called Šúvalky, there are several groups of rocks, and unknown signs are carved into one of them. We did not find them at the first attempt, but the second was more successful. The rock, about a metre high and a metre long, revealed its secret to us. At first sight we thought of Bodiná, where there are similar signs, though these are smaller. On a nearby rock a circle is carved, probably representing the sun, which suggests a possible cult place of our ancestors. While the Bodiná inscription has been known for a hundred years, the people here knew about the signs for roughly the same length of time, but said of them that there were just some sort of inscriptions there, and perhaps that is why nobody took any interest in them.“

blocks.alt: Mysterious signs carved into rocks in the Váh region

children.text: Štefan Meliš did not, however, keep the discovery to himself; he wrote about it in the magazine Historická revue. „I hoped that experts would take an interest in the signs and in deciphering them, but unfortunately, a year later nobody had got in touch.“ Will anyone be found who manages to decipher the signs before they are lost altogether in the weathering rock? Perhaps that would help to fill in the blank spaces in our history.
We also learn about the stone with the mysterious signs on Orgoňova Kýčera from a very interesting
legend recorded by Štefan Meliš

, about an ancient pagan priest – Orgoň, who was one of the last to resist Christianity, until in the end Perún himself took him. Orgoň was struck by lightning, and on the spot where it happened only a stone with mysterious carved inscriptions has remained ever since.

This year (2013) the archaeologist Peter Schreiber attempted an interpretation of the signs on Orgoňova Kýčera; in an article for the website of the village of Horná Mariková he states that „the slopes of Orgoňova Kýčera were in the past more deforested than they are today, which depended on human occupation. The hills therefore offered a good view over the wide surroundings of the Mariková and Papradno valleys, as well as views out into the Váh region. Purely theoretically, the signs carved into the rock on Orgoňova Kýčera could thus represent a kind of „map“ or „schematic plan“. The signs themselves consist of zigzag lines, small crosses, circles and semicircles. In the middle there is a zigzag line with four peaks. It could indicate the ridge of Kýčera together with the summits and spot heights of the surrounding hills: Suchovrch (774.9 m a.s.l.), Vrchoňa (883.0 m a.s.l.) and the unnamed spot height of 936.7 m a.s.l. east of Orgoňova Kýčera. The other carved signs, which are to the left and right of the zigzag line, could thus represent the hamlets in the wider surroundings of Kýčera. The signs could, however, have had a different function as well, as boundary marks defining the border between the Mariková and the Papradno valleys.“ At the same time he points out that this is only one of several possible interpretations, and that it cannot be ruled out that the signs are older than the 18th century mentioned. In this he refers to the attested occupation of Mariková in the Early Iron Age, the Roman period and the Middle Ages.
